content: Leonardo Martínez Moya founded the company together with other former dancers and teachers of the Conjunto Folklórico Nacional de Cuba.

Our aim is to teach, share and preserve traditional Cuban folkloric dance. Under the direction of Leonardo Martínez Moya and Giuliana Cassarisi, the maestros pass on what they learned in Havana to dancers and musicians from many countries.
In this way, the company is also a tribute to the Cuban people, and to the maestros, dancers and musicians who carried Cuban culture around the world before us.
Dancers from all over Europe and beyond, brought together by Cuban dance.
Every month we meet for a training weekend in a different European city.
Regular classes in technique and repertoire, and rehearsals for our shows.
We perform at festivals, cultural events and on tour.
We work with other artists, choreographers and musicians on new productions.
Workshops and events that bring in local dancers wherever we go.
We want to protect and share Cuba's dance and music traditions through performances, workshops and work with other artists.
Teaching is at the centre of what we do. Our programmes pass on Cuban dance technique and folklore to new generations of dancers in Europe.
We also document traditional Cuban dances, including choreographies, music and costumes, so that they can be passed on.

We regularly travel to Havana for our Encuentros. There we train with the maestros of the Conjunto Folklórico Nacional de Cuba and of Conjunto Ban Rarrá. In 2024 and 2025 we spent two weeks of classes in Havana.
Everyone starts in the academy. You learn the dances in depth, at your own pace, and you can stay as long as you like, even if you can't come every month.

Company members perform on stage across Europe. After at least three training weekends, the teachers decide if you join the company or stay in the academy a little longer. Members come every month and also rehearse at home.
What is the International Company of Cuban Dances?

A company of dancers from all over Europe, founded in 2022, who train and perform traditional Afro-Cuban folkloric dance. You can read about our teachers on the About page or see our classes on Instagram.
How can I join the Academy?

The academy is open to everyone who joins us for the first time. You can stay in the academy if you don't feel ready to perform yet, or if you can't come regularly. If you mainly want to train and improve, the academy is the place for you.
How can I join the Company?

There is no audition day. Let Leonardo or someone from the organisation know you are interested. You then join the academy classes for at least three training weekends while the teachers watch you dance. After that, they decide if you join the company or stay in the academy a little longer.

These are not beginner classes. You need to know the basics of Yoruba, Arará, Palo, Makuta, Yuka and Rumba, as we do not teach basic steps or rhythms. Ideally you have taken at least two years of classes. This applies to both the academy and the company.
I am a teacher, do I have to audition?
Yes. Many of you have danced for years or teach yourselves, but to keep it fair the process is the same for everyone.
Where do the trainings take place?
In a different European city every month, thanks to our students who help organise them. See the Trainings page for dates and venues.

Leonardo Moya, Sergio Larrinaga, Arelys Savón and Mireisi Morales, all former dancers of the Conjunto Folklórico Nacional de Cuba, where they also trained. In the 2026–2027 season they are joined by Javier Monier and Federico Núñez.
How long are the training weekends?

About 10 hours of classes over two days. We usually start on Saturday around midday or 1 pm and finish on Sunday around 5 pm, so people have time to travel. The timetable is published a week before each training.
What do you do during the trainings?

Usually a mix of singing, Yoruba technique, orisha dances, Palo, Arará and Rumba, plus popular dances such as mambo, cha-cha-chá and son, with live percussion. Company members also rehearse the choreographies for our shows.
We keep performing Raíces Cubanas around Europe and are working on a new show. We also perform at festivals and events during the year.
What is the level of commitment for company members?

When we are working towards a show, company members come every month. You can miss one training at most; if you need to miss more, talk to the teachers. You learn the choreographies and practise at home so we can use our time together well. Everyone dances in more than one choreography.
What does it cost and how do I sign up?
Tickets and ICCD T-shirts are sold on Weezevent. Early-bird tickets are the cheapest, and we always announce when the early-bird price ends.
Do I need to arrange my own accommodation?
Yes, everyone books their own travel and accommodation. If something is organised for the group, we'll share it in the WhatsApp group.
Who can I contact with more questions?
Join our WhatsApp group or send us a message on Instagram.

Leonardo Martínez Moya and Giuliana Cassarisi direct the company. A small team of dancers organises the trainings, shows and trips.
Dancers from all over Europe who share a love of Afro-Cuban dance. Together we perform traditional Cuban dances outside Cuba and help keep them alive.
Live drums and singing are part of every training and every show. These musicians played at the Raíces Cubanas premiere at the Arca Social Club in Rome on 25 May 2024.
We perform Afro-Cuban folklore and Cuban popular dances at festivals, theatres and cultural events across Europe, always with live drums and singing. Our full-length production is Raíces Cubanas.

A 90-minute dance-theatre show in two parts
Raíces Cubanas tells the story of Cuban music and dance, from its African roots to the Cuba of today. A 90-minute show with 20 to 30 dancers, live drums and singing.

The show was created by Leonardo Martínez Moya with Sergio Larrinaga, Mireisi Morales and Arelys Savón. It includes original choreographies from the early years of the Conjunto Folklórico Nacional de Cuba. It is presented with the Generación Abbilona Association.

The first part is about the Afro-Cuban religious world. We dance for the orishas Elegguá, Ogún, Yemayá, Changó and Oyá. We also show the crossing of enslaved Africans to Cuba, and how their beliefs and music became part of Cuban identity.

The second part is about Cuba's popular dances, from the birth of the Republic to today. Danzón, mambo, cha-cha-chá, son, rumba, the street vendors' calls (pregones) and carnival. It celebrates the mix of cultures that makes Cuba what it is.

Taught by former dancers of the Conjunto Folklórico Nacional de Cuba. One weekend a month, each time in a different European city, with live drums and singing.

ICCD was founded in 2022 by former dancers and teachers of the Conjunto Folklórico Nacional de Cuba. Today it brings together dancers from all over Europe. We train together every month, perform Cuban folkloric dance on stage and pass on what the maestros teach us.
Come for the dance. Stay for the people.

We are dancers from more than fifteen countries. Once a month we travel to a different city, share a studio for a weekend, eat together, and go home tired and happy. What started as classes has turned into friendships across Europe. We are here to learn, to perform, and to share Cuban music and dance.

Leonardo studied at the Escuela Nacional de Arte (ENA) and the Instituto Superior de Arte (ISA) in Havana. He was a principal dancer of the Conjunto Folklórico Nacional de Cuba for 25 years. As a choreographer there, he created the pieces Moforibale a Changó and Ochanigue.

In 2008 he moved to Italy, where he founded Proyecto Lucumí. He has taught in more than 30 countries. He teaches Afro-Cuban dances (Yoruba, Congo, Arará, Abakuá), rumba, Cuban popular dances, campesino dances and Cuban salsa, as well as contemporary and folkloric technique.

He also teaches at international festivals.

Arelys graduated from the Escuela Nacional de Arte and the Instituto Superior de Arte (ISA) in Cuba. She was a soloist and teacher with the Conjunto Folklórico Nacional de Cuba, touring Europe, Japan, Mexico, the Dominican Republic, the United States and many other countries, and worked in television, film and modelling.

She has lived in Italy since 2004. She is a member of the Italian Dance Sport Federation, where she judges competitions, and a first-level MIDAS – ASC Danza teacher. She teaches Cuban dance in Italy and across Europe.

She is a member of UNEAC (the Union of Writers and Artists of Cuba) and of CID-UNESCO. She wrote the book Danzas Arará: Tradición Ewe-Fon en Cuba, about the cosmology, songs, rhythms and steps of the Arará dances. It is the first title of her own series, Raíces en Movimiento.

Sergio was a principal dancer and choreographer with the Conjunto Folklórico Nacional de Cuba. During his long career he also taught and choreographed at the Teatro América in Havana and directed the company Yoruba Andabo.

He now lives in Italy, where he is a member of the Federazione Professionale di Danza (FPD), and teaches Cuban and Afro-Cuban dance around the world.

He leads the academy for popular and folkloric dance Raíces de Fuego in Mestre (Venice), where he teaches timba, orisha dances, palo, rumba and abakuá, together with percussion and the history of the dances.

Mireisi trained at the Instituto Superior de Arte (ISA) and was a first dancer of the Conjunto Folklórico Nacional de Cuba. At our trainings she teaches technique and orisha dances. In Rome she co-leads the project Raíces y Elegancia.

Javier comes from the Conjunto Folklórico Nacional de Cuba. Today he is the artistic director and choreographer of the Compañía Cubana de Danza Javier Monier in Madrid. He created the show Fiesta de Reyes, a tribute to the Cuban violinist José Claudio Brindis de Salas, and teaches Afro-Cuban dance, rumba, Afro-contemporary and timba.

Federico comes from the Tropicana cabaret in Havana. He is known for the Cuban cabaret style and modern Cuban dance. He gives cabaret masterclasses at festivals such as Festival Cultura Cubana, teaches Cuban dance technique in Rome and choreographs for the stage.
